THOUGHT: This 47-year-old female presents with a 3-week subacute illness featuring fatigue, low-grade fever, abdominal pain, nausea, dark urine, and now objective findings of mild scleral icterus and hepatomegaly with hepatic tenderness. Laboratory evaluation reveals marked elevation of transaminases (AST 488 U/L, ALT 798 U/L), indicating significant hepatocellular injury. Total bilirubin is elevated (3.6 mg/dL) with predominant direct (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia (2.4 mg/dL), consistent with hepatocellular or cholestatic liver dysfunction — but the disproportionately high ALT/AST (ALT > AST) and absence of alkaline phosphatase elevation (72 U/L, normal) strongly favor hepatocellular injury over cholestasis. The infectious serology is highly specific: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) positive, hepatitis B envelope antigen (HBeAg) positive, and hepatitis B core IgG antibody positive — all indicate active, replicative chronic hepatitis B infection. The positive HBV core IgG (not IgM) suggests this is not an acute *primary* HBV infection (which would typically show HBc IgM positive), but rather a reactivation or flare of chronic HBV — especially plausible given her occupational exposure (nursing assistant in rehab facility), daily alcohol use (a known cofactor for HBV progression and liver injury), and underlying type 2 diabetes (associated with increased risk of fibrosis and poorer outcomes in viral hepatitis). Her dark urine reflects conjugated hyperbilirubinemia; fatigue, fever, and right upper quadrant pain are classic systemic and hepatic manifestations of hepatitis flare. Anemia (Hb 10.6 g/dL) may reflect chronic disease or mild hemolysis, but is not dominant. No evidence of autoimmune hepatitis (no IgG elevation or autoantibodies reported), no features of drug-induced liver injury (no recent new medications), and negative HCV and resolved (IgG-only) HAV make other etiologies less likely. Alcohol use contributes but cannot alone explain such profound transaminitis and jaundice without concomitant alcoholic hepatitis (which usually shows AST > ALT, often >2:1 ratio, and more prominent MCV elevation — neither present here). Thus, the serologic and biochemical profile overwhelmingly points to hepatitis B virus reactivation or flare.

DIAGNOSIS: Chronic hepatitis B virus infection with acute exacerbation (hepatitis B flare).
